extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, and publishers who apply Chicago Manual of Style rules
extracted.subtask_description: Style and editorial rules for formatting quotations, dialogue, ellipses, interpolations, and attribution in prose, poetry, drama, interviews, and field notes, as given by the Chicago Manual of Style (chapter on Quotations and Dialogue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Double or Single Quotation Marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted words, phrases, and sentences run into the text are enclosed in double quotation marks. Single quotation marks enclose quotations within quotations; double marks, quotations within these; and so on. (The practice in the United Kingdom and elsewhere is often the reverse.) When the material quoted consists entirely of a quotation within a quotation, only one set of quotation marks need be employed (usually double quotation marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For permissible changes from single to double quotation marks and vice versa, see 13.7 (item 1); see also 13.63. For dialogue, see 13.39.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of Terminal Punctuation with Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points and question marks are placed just within the set of quotation marks ending the element to which such terminal punctuation belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note placement relative to closing single and double quotation marks; see also 6.9-11 for related punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation Marks in Block Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Material set off as a block quotation is not enclosed in quotation marks, but quoted matter within the block quotation is enclosed in double quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An author or editor who changes a run-in quotation to a block quotation must delete the opening and closing quotation marks and change any internal ones appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations of More than One Paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted material of more than one paragraph should be presented as a block quotation if at all possible. If run in, a quotation mark is needed at the beginning of the quotation and at the beginning of each new paragraph but at the end of only the final paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each successive paragraph must begin on a new line, as in the original. Same practice for dialogue when one speaker’s remarks extend over more than one paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations within Quotations across Paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted material that contains an interior quotation that runs for more than one paragraph should be presented as a block quotation if at all possible; original quotation marks should be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If run in, a single quotation mark appears at the beginning and at the end of the interior quotation as a whole, and both double and single marks appear before each new paragraph belonging to the interior quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting More Than One Stanza of Poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetry quotation that spans more than one stanza should be presented as an extract if at all possible; if it must be run in, two slashes (//), with a space before and after, should appear between stanzas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the use of the slash between run-in lines of poetry, see 13.29; presenting as an extract (block) is preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting Letters in Their Entirety
rubrics_metrics.description: A letter quoted in its entirety should be set off as a block quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If run in, it should carry an opening quotation mark before the first line (including the salutation) and before each new paragraph (each beginning on a new line); a closing quotation mark appears only after the last line (often the signature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epigraphs (Quotation Marks Omitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks are not used around epigraphs; like block quotations, epigraphs receive a distinctive typographic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epigraphs often set in smaller type or indented; treatment of sources varies but multiple epigraphs in the same work should receive consistent treatment (see 13.70-72).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative Initials and Opening Quotation Marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chapter or section opens with a large raised or dropped initial letter that begins a run-in quotation, the opening quotation mark is often omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the opening quotation mark is included, it should appear in the same size and with the same vertical alignment as the regular text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maxims and Questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxims, mottoes, rules, and other familiar expressions are sometimes enclosed in quotation marks; questions that do not require quotation marks are discussed elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 6.41, 7.62 for maxims and 6.42, 6.69 for questions that do not require quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Discourse and Dialogue Formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct discourse or dialogue is traditionally enclosed in quotation marks. A change in speaker is usually indicated by a new paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one speech occupies more than a paragraph, opening quotation marks are needed at the beginning of each new paragraph, with a closing quotation mark placed at the end of only the final paragraph (see also 13.32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-Word Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Single words such as yes, no, where, how, and why, when used singly, are not enclosed in quotation marks except in direct discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex: Ezra always answered yes; but in direct reply: "Yes," he replied weakly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faltering Speech / Incomplete Thoughts (Ellipsis Use)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis may be used to suggest faltering or fragmented speech accompanied by confusion or insecurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note relative positions of ellipses and other punctuation; compare with editorial-omission ellipses (13.50-58). Interruptions or abrupt changes in thought are usually indicated by em dashes (see 6.87).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interruptions Indicated by Em Dashes
rubrics_metrics.description: Interruptions or abrupt changes in thought are usually indicated by em dashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Em dashes are distinct from ellipses used for faltering speech; see examples and 6.87.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to Quotation Marks
rubrics_metrics.description: In some languages, em dashes are used to present dialogue; guillemets (« ») are another alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See examples in chapter 11 for language-specific treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unspoken / Interior Discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought, imagined dialogue, and other internal discourse may be enclosed in quotation marks or not, according to context or the writer’s preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a thought begins midsentence, it normally begins with a capital letter. Stream-of-consciousness may require no quotation marks at all (see Joyce example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerals in Direct Discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: In quoting directly from spoken sources or writing direct discourse, numbers that might otherwise be rendered as numerals can often be spelled out; editorial discretion is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Years can usually be rendered as numerals, as can trade names that include numerals. For dialogue with many large numbers, use numerals for practicality (see 9.2, 9.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect Discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect discourse, which paraphrases dialogue, takes no quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex: Tom told Huck they had to do it that way because the books said so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drama Formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In plays, the speaker’s name is usually set in a font distinct from the dialogue (caps or small caps); the dialogue is not enclosed in quotation marks and is usually set with hanging indents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage directions are usually italicized. Hanging indents aid identification of speakers; names are usually followed by a period or colon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared Lines and Runover Lines in Verse Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: A single line of verse shared between two speakers should be presented such that the second line continues where the first has left off; runover lines in poetry may be indicated by an indent of one em or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format examples provided for shared lines between speakers (see 13.48-49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcription of Discussions and Interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcription of discussions or interviews is treated much the same way as drama: interjections such as 'laughter' are italicized and enclosed in brackets; paragraph indents are usually preferred to hanging indents; names may be abbreviated after first appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors' previously unpublished transcriptions can be edited for capitalization, spelling, and minor slips; significant alterations should be explained in a note or preface. Previously published transcriptions should be quoted as in the original source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case Studies and Ethnographic Field Notes
rubrics_metrics.description: An author’s transcriptions of unpublished ethnographic field notes or case-study material need not be presented verbatim; such material should be edited for consistency in spelling, capitalization, punctuation, treatment of numbers, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous subjects should generally be presented under pseudonyms and noted as such; modifications intended to maintain anonymity are acceptable but must not lead to misrepresentation—editors should query authors when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses Defined (General)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis is a series of three dots used to signal the omission of a word, phrase, line, paragraph, or more from a quoted passage; Chicago style is to use three spaced periods (but see 13.53).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dots must appear together on the same line (use nonbreaking spaces); authors may use the Unicode three-dot ellipsis (U+2026), but editors will replace with spaced periods. Ellipses may also indicate faltering speech (see 13.41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of Skewing Meaning with Ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: Care must be exercised when eliding text to ensure that the sense of the original is not lost or misrepresented; a deletion must not result in a statement alien to the original material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ellipses should not be used to join two statements that are far apart in the original. Accuracy of sense and emphasis must accompany accuracy of transcription.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Not to Use an Ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses are normally not used (1) before the first word of a quotation, even if the beginning of the original sentence has been omitted; or (2) after the last word of a quotation, even if the end of the original sentence has been omitted, unless the sentence as quoted is deliberately incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 13.55 for deliberately incomplete sentences exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses with Periods (Sentence-End Omissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is added before an ellipsis to indicate the omission of the end of a sentence, unless the sentence is deliberately incomplete; similarly, a period at the end of a sentence in the original is retained before an ellipsis indicating the omission of material immediately following the period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What precedes and, normally, what follows the four dots should be grammatically complete sentences as quoted. The first word after an ellipsis is capitalized if it begins a new grammatical sentence; some works require such capitalization changes to be bracketed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses with Other Punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Other punctuation appearing in the original—a comma, colon, semicolon, question mark, or exclamation point—may precede or follow an ellipsis (except when a period precedes the ellipsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to include the additional mark depends on whether keeping it aids comprehension or is required for the grammar. When the omission precedes the mark, use a nonbreaking space between the ellipsis and that punctuation to prevent the mark from carrying over to the next line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses at Ends of Deliberately Incomplete Sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis alone (three dots with no additional period) is used at the end of a quoted sentence that is deliberately left grammatically incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No space intervenes between a final ellipsis point and a closing quotation mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses for Omission of Whole or Partial Paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission of one or more paragraphs within a quotation is indicated by a period followed by an ellipsis at the end of the paragraph preceding the omitted part; if the first part of a paragraph is omitted, a paragraph indent and an ellipsis appear before the first quoted word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paragraph ends with an incomplete sentence, use only the three-dot ellipsis at its end. It is possible to use an ellipsis both at the end of one paragraph and at the beginning of the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses in Poetry and Verse Drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of the end of a line of verse is indicated by a period followed by an ellipsis if what precedes them is a complete grammatical sentence; otherwise, only the three-dot ellipsis is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of a full line or several consecutive lines within a quoted poem or verse drama is indicated by one line of widely spaced dots approximately the length of the line above (or of the missing line). See examples in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketed Ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: In contexts where ellipses appear in the original or where many ellipses would otherwise be inserted, authors may bracket their own ellipses to indicate omissions in quoted text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules are same as for unbracketed ellipses except a period is placed before or after the ellipsis depending on its placement in the original. Format inside brackets: bracket-period-space-period-space-period-bracket; a space appears before an opening bracket and after a closing bracket unless followed by punctuation. Nonbreaking spaces are needed for the internal spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolations and Clarifications for Missing or Illegible Words
rubrics_metrics.description: When reproducing or quoting from a document with missing or illegible words, an author may use ellipses, a bracketed comment or guess (sometimes with a question mark), or both; if ellipses alone are used their function must be explained in the text or a note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a bracketed gloss comes from a different source, cite that source in a note. A 2-em dash, sometimes with an interpolated guess, may also be used for missing material; consistency and explanation (in prefatory material or a note) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bracketed Clarifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Insertions made in quoted material to clarify an ambiguity, provide a missing word or letters, correct an error, or give the original word in translation are enclosed in brackets (never parentheses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such interpolations should be kept to a minimum to avoid irritating or distracting readers. See examples and 6.99, 13.12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sic
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Sic' (italicized, in brackets) may be inserted following a word misspelled or wrongly used in the original to indicate the error is in the source and not the transcription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use [sic] only when relevant to call attention to such matters; do not use merely to call attention to unconventional spellings—explain those in a note or prefatory material. Avoid repeated sics when reproducing material with many errors or variant spellings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italics Added / Emphasis Added Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An author wishing to call attention to a word or phrase in quoted material by italicizing it must tell readers what has been done by formulas such as 'italics mine,' 'italics added,' 'emphasis added,' or 'emphasis mine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally note if italics in a quotation were in the original using phrases such as 'italics in the original.' Place this information in parentheses following the quotation or in a source note; consistency throughout a work is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolations that Include Quotation Marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A bracketed or parenthetical interpolation that includes quotation marks appearing inside material already enclosed in quotation marks does not require the usual double/single switching rule; the quotation marks within the brackets may remain double.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided where bracketed interpolation contains double quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Parentheses with In-Text Citations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the source of a direct quotation is not given in a note, it is usually placed in the text in parentheses; the source may follow the quotation or come earlier if it fits more smoothly into the introductory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section supplements notes and bibliography rules (chapter 14). Examples show full and short forms suitable for short works with no notes or for frequent quotations of a single work. See also author-date guidance in chapter 15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full In-Text Citation Format
rubrics_metrics.description: An entire source may be given in parentheses immediately following a quotation (full bibliographic details), or some data may be worked into the text with details confined to parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 14.23 for proper bibliographic form. Examples show full citation elements (author, title, publisher, date, page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortened Citations and Ibid.
rubrics_metrics.description: If a second passage from the same source is quoted close to the first and no intervening quotation from a different source exists, the author’s name or 'ibid.' (set in roman) may be used in the second parenthetical reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago prefers the 'author, page' form as less ambiguous, though 'ibid.' may be appropriate if used consistently. Avoid overuse; for extended repeated references, a parenthetical page number alone may suffice. If another source intervenes, include a shortened reference with title as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent Reference to a Single Source Cited in a Note
rubrics_metrics.description: In a work containing notes, the full citation of a source may be given in a note at first mention, with subsequent citations made parenthetically in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method suits literary studies using frequent quotations from a single source. Where multiple editions/titles are used, indicate edition/title in parenthetical references or devise abbreviations and include a list of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation Following Source of Run-In Quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: After a run-in quotation, the source is usually given after the closing quotation mark, followed by the rest of the surrounding sentence (including any comma, semicolon, colon, or dash; but see 13.69) or the final punctuation of that sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A parenthetical reference need not immediately follow the quotation as long as it is clear what it belongs to. Examples illustrate placement relative to sentence punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation Preceding Source of Run-In Quotation (Question/Exclamation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation comes at the end of a sentence and is itself a question or an exclamation, that punctuation is retained within the quotation marks, and a period is still added after the closing parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: quotation ending with a question mark inside quotes followed by (page) and then a period after the closing parenthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical Source Following Block Quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of a block quotation is given in parentheses at the end of the quotation and in the same type size; the opening parenthesis appears after the final punctuation mark of the quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No period precedes or follows the closing parenthesis. Shortened references are treated similarly; qualifiers like 'line,' 'vol.,' or 'p.' are lowercased if required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical Citations with Poetry Extracts
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid interfering with a poem's layout, parenthetical citations following poetry extracts are dropped to the line below the last line of the quotation and may be centered on the last letter of the longest line or set flush with the left margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An additional line space may be added; other positions are possible provided consistency and clarity are preserved.
